title: Working Through a Problem Breakdown
summary: Use one repeatable route from a vague prompt to a defended design.
keyPoints: Pick three features: the core flow, the architecture-changing feature, and the constraint that could break the design.
Turn prompt nouns into entities, verbs into API calls, and promises into non-functional requirements.
Draw the smallest end-to-end design before adding caches, queues, or extra services.
Use the hard part of the prompt to choose the deep dive: fan-out, concurrency, ranking, sync, or correctness.
A 45-minute answer needs a stated plan for scope, numbers, API, design, deep dives, and failure.
Review with a rubric instead of adding more boxes.

complexity.note: State what is out of scope.

commonMistakes: Spending most of the time on requirements and never drawing the system.
Choosing a database or broker before naming the access pattern.
Listing technologies without explaining the role each one plays.
Skipping the deep dive because the high-level overview looks complete.
interviewNotes: Open with the three features and the out-of-scope list.
Say the read and write estimates before choosing components.
Trace one write and one read through the diagram.
Reserve time for one hard part, its failure path, and its trade-off.
Finish with the metric you would watch and what changes at 10x.

checkYourself.question: Why choose only three features at the start?
checkYourself.answer: A short scope leaves time for the API, data model, and deep dives. A broad scope usually produces a shallow design with no defended trade-offs.

checkYourself.question: What makes a good deep-dive topic?
checkYourself.answer: It is the part of the prompt where scale or correctness breaks the simple design, such as celebrity fan-out, double booking, ordering, or sync conflicts.

checkYourself.question: What should a self-review rubric catch?
checkYourself.answer: It should catch missing numbers, an untraced request path, an overview that never goes deeper, and the absence of a failure or monitoring plan.
